Build or buy: a practical way to decide

Custom software is neither always better nor always more expensive. How to tell when an off-the-shelf product is enough, and when it is costing you more than it saves.

Every business reaches a point where an existing tool no longer fits. The question that follows is whether to find a better product or build something. As a company that builds software, we should say plainly: buying is frequently the right answer.

When buying makes sense

If the process is common across many businesses, such as payroll, bookkeeping, email or basic ticketing, mature products exist and are maintained by teams far larger than any you would fund. Adapting your process slightly to fit a good product is usually cheaper than building software to preserve a habit.

When building makes sense

  • The process is a real point of difference, and a generic tool would flatten it.
  • You are paying for several products and stitching them together by hand every day.
  • Licence costs scale with users or volume in a way that will soon exceed the cost of ownership.
  • You need integration or control that available products do not offer.

The option people forget

It is rarely all or nothing. A common and sensible pattern is to buy the commodity parts and build only the piece that is specific to you, connecting the two through APIs. You get a maintained foundation and a custom layer small enough to own comfortably.

Count the whole cost

Compare the options over several years, not at the point of purchase. For a product, include licences, configuration, training and the manual work it leaves behind. For custom software, include hosting, maintenance and the changes you will inevitably want. An honest comparison often settles the argument.
